chapters.title: Language for interacting with others, and text structure

points.title: Language and relationships
points.brief: How formal or casual our words are, and how we address people, shows and shapes the relationship, such as between a student and a principal or two friends.

points.title: Evaluating with simile and metaphor
points.brief: A review can judge through comparison, such as calling a film a rollercoaster, which adds a layer of meaning a plain judgement lacks.

points.title: Hybrid texts
points.brief: A hybrid text mixes genres or text types, such as a novel told through diary entries and emails, to create new effects.

points.title: Building a strong paragraph
points.brief: A strong body paragraph makes a claim in its topic sentence, then supports it with examples and evidence and explains how they prove the claim.

points.title: Using quotations as evidence
points.brief: A short quotation woven into your own sentence backs up a claim, and it needs an explanation of what it shows.

points.title: Embedded clauses
points.brief: An embedded clause sits inside a sentence, often starting with who, which or that, to add information about a noun.

points.title: Nominalisation
points.brief: Nominalisation turns a verb or adjective into a noun, such as decide into decision, which makes writing sound more formal and less personal.

points.title: Using semicolons
points.brief: A semicolon joins two closely linked main clauses without a conjunction, and it separates items in a list when the items already contain commas.

points.title: Using dashes
points.brief: A dash can add an extra idea, an aside or a dramatic pause, and a pair of dashes works like brackets but draws more attention.

points.title: Intertextual references in images
points.brief: A visual text can borrow from a well-known image, such as a poster copying a famous painting, so viewers bring that meaning to the new image.

points.title: Intertextual references in literature
points.brief: A text can refer to another text, such as a fairy tale, myth or famous story, and readers who notice it gain a deeper understanding.

points.title: Academic vocabulary
points.brief: Academic texts use words such as analyse, significant, consequently and evidence, which are more precise and formal than everyday words.

points.title: Texts represent values
points.brief: The ideas and points of view in a literary text can show what a person or group believes is right, fair or important.

points.title: Values in First Nations Australian literature
points.brief: Literature by First Nations Australian authors can share values such as connection to Country, family and community, and readers consider the context these come from.

points.title: An author's style
points.brief: Style is the way an author typically writes, through choices of words, sentence lengths, devices and structure.

points.title: Positioning the reader
points.brief: Writers and creators use word choice, detail and images to lead readers to feel a certain way about a character, event or issue.

points.title: Sentence patterns and tone
points.brief: Short, sharp sentences can build tension, while long, flowing sentences can create a calm or dreamy tone.

points.title: Repetition for effect
points.brief: Repeating a word, phrase or sentence pattern stresses an idea, builds rhythm and makes a passage memorable.

points.title: Sensory imagery
points.brief: Imagery that appeals to sight, sound, smell, taste and touch helps readers experience a scene and creates mood.

points.title: Choosing devices for an effect
points.brief: In their own writing, students pick devices to suit the effect they want, such as short sentences for suspense or exaggeration for humour.

chapters.title: Texts in context and interacting with others

points.title: Texts reflect contexts
points.brief: A text shows the time, place and society it was made in, through its language, its attitudes and what it takes for granted.

points.title: Stated and implied meanings
points.brief: A speaker states some ideas directly and implies others, and a listener can support or challenge both.

points.title: Formal and informal register
points.brief: Register is how formal language is. A speech to a school assembly needs a more formal register than a chat with friends.

points.title: Sources and quotations in a text
points.brief: Writers quote experts and cite sources to make a text seem reliable, and readers check who the source is and whether it can be trusted.

points.title: Persuasive devices
points.brief: Persuasive texts use devices such as rhetorical questions, emotive words, inclusive language and statistics to win readers over.

points.title: How authors organise ideas
points.brief: Authors can organise ideas as a problem and solution, a comparison, or from least to most important, to shape what readers think.

points.title: Evaluating ideas in texts
points.brief: Readers question a text's ideas by asking what evidence supports them and what has been left out.

points.title: Elaborating ideas
points.brief: Writers expand an idea with an example, an explanation, a detail or a comparison, so the reader understands it fully.

points.title: Structure of a persuasive essay
points.brief: A persuasive essay states a position in the introduction, gives one argument per body paragraph with evidence, and restates the position in the conclusion.

points.title: Homophones
points.brief: Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning, such as their, there and they're, so the meaning tells you which to write.

points.title: Spelling strategies for new words
points.brief: Breaking a word into syllables and parts, and using known spelling rules, helps students spell and learn unfamiliar words.
